Funding goal: Expand its team, increase installations of its AI-powered waste monitoring technology and develop new applications across the waste management chain to improve recycling efficiency.

Investor: Superhero Capital with NGL Ventures and the angels who joined the round: Jussi Pyörre, Kristoffer Abell and Jakob Lilholm
Funding goal: Advance its unified database technology for cloud and offline environments and hire specialised engineers to simplify data infrastructure for software developers.

Founders: Niclas Matthias and Dr. Paul Matthias  
Lead investor: Investment Advisory Club Düsseldorf - IACD e.V.

What can founders learn from these funding rounds?
These investments highlight how early-stage capital supports the transition from promising technology to commercially scalable businesses.
Across different sectors, startups are directing funding toward three priorities:
- Product development: Strengthening technology and building differentiated solutions.
- Market expansion: Reaching new customers and entering new markets.
- Team growth: Hiring specialised talent to support innovation and commercial execution.

For founders preparing to raise capital, a compelling product alone is not enough. Investors also evaluate founder-market fit, commercial traction, scalability and a clear strategy for deploying capital.

Over half the VP placements we make across Europe never have an open job posting on LinkedIn.

There is no application link, no intake form, and no celebratory company announcement that the seat is vacant.

Most senior professionals spend their week refreshing the same public job boards, operating under the assumption that executive hiring runs on volume. Behind the scenes, the most strategic decisions inside a scaleup happen far away from the feed for three operational reasons:

1. Confidential replacement searches.
The company needs to replace an executive who is currently in the seat running day-to-day operations. Going public with the role would destabilize internal teams, spook enterprise clients during contract renewals, and alert competitors.

2. Protecting market narrative.
A scaleup in the middle of a Series B raise or expanding into a new European market cannot afford to signal vulnerability. Broadcasting that you lost your Head of Sales or CTO in the middle of that cycle creates unnecessary friction with investors.

3. The collapse of traditional inbound screening under AI automation.
The moment a senior leadership title goes live on LinkedIn, it attracts 400 generic, bot-generated applications within 48 hours. No serious founder or hiring committee has the bandwidth to sift through automated noise for a €120k+ strategic hire.

The practical takeaway is direct: public job boards show only a fraction of the executive opportunities actually moving in the market.

The most critical conversations happen privately, through structured market mapping and direct outreach to operators who have already proven their ability to deliver at that specific stage of growth.

If your career transition strategy relies entirely on responding to public postings, you are competing in the wrong room.

Build visibility with the people who track your market quietly. At the executive level, the best conversations start months before a job exists on paper.

Hey Wispr Flow, maybe you saw this, maybe you didn’t. So I’m putting it out to the whole world now. 💜 

I’m Nimz, and I’ve been the new kid in more than 11 schools. Pune, Ambala, Bangalore. My parents’ postings kept us moving, and somewhere along the way, starting over stopped scaring me and started feeling like home. 

Then came University of Nottingham. I moved countries for my MSc, and the first months were hard. Nothing worked the way I was used to, and I had to learn to think all over again. I caught up, made friends, and fell completely in love with the city. Then London, an HR internship at Habib Bank, and a mentor who is still a dear friend today. 

And then London said no. For nearly six months I couldn’t find a job, and I won’t pretend that was easy. So I taught myself Power BI and Tableau and kept building. John Lewis Partnership gave me a six month contract and a crash course in bulk hiring, until my visa expired and I had to come back to India. 

Coming home was a difficult time. I missed the UK, I wasn’t sure I’d cope, but I kept going. At B4uLeap I got my first taste of tech hiring while we built a GCC, until it was acquired and my role became redundant. 

Then came Abstract Group, where I stopped just recruiting and started building. A talent map across 13 Indian cities. A requisition workflow I built from scratch. KSA market research. Recruitment metrics and candidate experience, all in one place. Those are the things I’m proudest of, and they’re the reason I know I’d be a great hire for any organisation that wants someone who builds, not just fills seats. 

Then life threw another curveball, an unfortunate mass layoff closed that chapter at Abstract Group. It was brief, but it was a great one, and I’m grateful for the time I got to work with AI tools there. So here I am, looking for my next best opportunity. I do my best work in strong, close teams, and I’m hoping to find mine. If you are a hiring manager looking for a talent like me, I am all ears  😄 

Somewhere in all of this, I found Wispr Flow. I spoke this entire portfolio into existence with it, and built the whole thing myself as an artifact. Swipe through and you’ll find my story in six chapters, what I tested, a few ideas I have for Flow in India, and a small app I talked into existence in minutes. 

To Tanay Kothari and the Wispr Flow team : thank you for making something that made me feel this capable. Whether or not this ever turns into a conversation, I’m so glad I got to build alongside you. And if my story speaks to you, I’d love to talk. 🫶

I just finished Strategic Human Resource Management in the MBA program at Guanghua School of Management, Peking University. 

I went in half expecting HR to be the department that handles contracts and vacation days. I was wrong. The course spent most of its time on a harder question: how a company's people decisions should follow from its strategy, and why so many companies do it the other way around. What stayed with me most is how fast AI is moving into this field. Screening CVs, writing job descriptions, planning onboarding, predicting who might quit next. Work that used to take an HR team weeks now takes a model an afternoon. 
It's also a little scary. A screening model learns from a company's past hiring decisions. If those decisions favored one university, one gender or one type of CV, the model treats that as the definition of a good candidate.
What worries me is the scale. One biased recruiter affects the people they interview. A biased model makes the same mistake thousands of times a day, and the candidates it filters out never learn why.

The fastest way I ever slowed a business down was by hiring.

We were winning work faster than we could deliver it, so I doubled the team in a month, and it felt like the most logical decision I’d ever made. (Just to be clear, this was before the AI Hype)

Within weeks I was drowning, trying to deliver the work and train an army of new hires at the same time. I’d paid for more hands and bought myself a second full-time job, because we’d never built a system for how the work got done.

That’s younger me in the photo and I still love her, she had no grey hairs and looked on point with no sleep and a solid hangover! For many years in business, the flex was how many hours you could work and how big your team was, because that’s what made you a “big” company. These days it’s how efficient you can be, how much tech you can utilise and whether you can get it done from anywhere. (Of course, revenue and profit counts as well)

The old flex dies hard though and we still see the same reflex with clients all the time. A big contract lands, the team is stretched and a job spec starts doing the rounds. More often than not the people they hire are perfectly good, which makes the real problem harder to see.

Be honest with yourself for a second: how much of the way your business runs exists anywhere other than in people’s heads?

Throwing bodies at an un-systematised problem doesn’t fix it, it just gives the chaos more hands. That isn’t a people problem, it’s a design problem.

The method I follow as a founder now is automate, delegate or drop. Before I reach for a new hire, I decide what can be automated, what can be handed to someone who owns it and what shouldn’t be getting done at all. I’m not against hiring, I just follow an order that works exceptionally well for me and my clients.

Headcount doesn’t fix a systems problem, it just makes it more expensive.

What’s the one thing on your plate right now that should already be automated, delegated or dropped? If you need some help deciding, let’s chat.

4 in 10 GitHub PRs now start with an AI agent. 

GitHub's Octoverse report, out last week, says more than 40% of pull requests in September started with an agent. In March it was 17%.

For those of us working remotely from Nigeria, that changes the job. Writing code is getting cheaper. Judging code is not.

I use coding agents every day. The skill that saves me isn't prompting. It's reviewing. And I learnt it teaching beginners at TechyJaunt, reading code that was confident and still wrong.

My review questions are the same for a junior's PR or an agent's:

1. What happens if this runs twice? (webhooks, retries, double charges)
2. What did it change that I didn't ask for? (tests, config, package.json)
3. What happens if the network fails halfway?

If you're job hunting, don't only show what you built. Show a PR where you caught what the agent missed. That tells a hiring manager more than another to-do app.

I'm open to remote senior backend roles and contract work on payments and bookings. My DMs are open.

Thinking about hiring a reverse recruiter for your job search?

Before you pay, understand what the service can actually cost.

In 2026, full-service reverse recruiting can range from roughly:

→ $1,500–$4,000 per month  
→ $1,000–$15,000+ for flat-fee packages  
→ Several thousand dollars for executive programs  
→ Plus, in some cases, 8%–10% of your first-year salary as a success fee  

That last part can become expensive very quickly.

For example:

A 10% success fee on a $100,000 offer = $10,000

A 10% success fee on a $150,000 offer = $15,000

And that may be on top of monthly fees.

So what are you actually paying for?

A reverse recruiter may help with:

• Finding target roles  
• Resume and LinkedIn optimization  
• Submitting applications  
• Hiring-manager outreach  
• Interview preparation  
• Salary negotiation  

But not every provider includes everything.

Before signing a contract, ask:

→ Is there a monthly retainer?  
→ Is there a success fee?  
→ What salary amount is that percentage calculated on?  
→ Is there a minimum commitment?  
→ Are resume and LinkedIn services refundable?  
→ Are there application limits?  
→ What does the guarantee actually mean?  
→ Does “guarantee” mean a refund or simply more service time?  

A reverse recruiter can make sense if:

• You’re targeting senior or executive roles  
• Your search requires networking and direct outreach  
• You have very little time to manage the process  
• You need strategic career support  

But if your biggest problem is simply:

Finding relevant jobs → Tailoring resumes → Submitting applications → Tracking everything

You may not need to spend thousands of dollars.

That’s where application-focused services like FlashFire can be a more affordable alternative.

FlashFire helps with:

→ Finding targeted job opportunities  
→ AI-assisted resume optimization  
→ Job-specific resume tailoring  
→ A team manually submitting applications on your behalf  
→ Tracking applications in one place  
→ Additional career support depending on the plan  

The key is simple:

Don’t pay for a $10,000+ service if you only need help with application execution.

Northwood announced on 2 November that it has closed a $375 million Series C to expand the ground network connecting satellites to Earth.

The financing will support delivery on existing contracts, hiring and the buildout of a shared network serving satellites in multiple orbits. Northwood reports six deployed sites across two continents and a new manufacturing facility in Torrance, California.

The business model addresses a practical constraint: satellite operators need reliable ground capacity to move data. By booking capacity on shared infrastructure, they can avoid building a dedicated network themselves. The new capital gives Northwood resources to scale both manufacturing and service delivery.

Northwood is part of SignalRank’s publicly disclosed portfolio. SM Capital’s exposure is indirect, through Innovation Global’s investment in SignalRank.

Our Mediterranean perspective: resilient connectivity supports digital services, remote operations and the movement of data used by AI across Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and the Gulf. We see shared ground infrastructure as relevant to these needs. This is our analysis of the business model; the announcement does not establish a Northwood deployment in the region.

In an interview, "I don't know" can be the best thing a person says. It really depends on what they say next.

Experience matters, and we're not brushing it off. But a confident wrong answer can cost more than an honest gap.

Think about it this way. Viceroy NM works under federal rules, where a wrong answer in a proposal can cost a contract. Trunnion AI builds software that acts on its own, where a wrong guess can reach real records. In both places, someone who says "I'm not sure, let me check" gives the team a chance to catch the problem. Someone who guesses might hide it until it's expensive.

Well, the usual question is "Tell me about your experience." The one we like better is "Tell me about a time you didn't know the answer. What did you do next?"

That's how we think about it at Duskbridge, and it isn't a proven rule for every role.

If you hire, try that second question once. Listen to how the person describes the gap. Do they get defensive, or curious?

Advertising salaries on job adverts by law is really going to shake things up❄️

And it could blow the lid off one of recruitment's biggest dirty little secrets.

After 31 years in recruitment, I know exactly why so many employers don't want salaries advertised.

Because the person they're trying to recruit is often going to earn MORE than the person already doing the job!

Same role. Same skills. Same team.

Different salary.

The software engineer who's been loyal for five years.

The developer who built the platform the entire business relies on.

The engineering manager holding everything together.

All potentially earning LESS than the new starter sitting next to them.

And the business knows it.

Every week, clients ask us to keep salaries off adverts.

Why?

Because publishing the salary opens a MASSIVE can of worms internally.

Suddenly people start asking awkward questions.

"Hang on, why is the new starter earning £15k more than me?"

And that's when HR and Finance start sweating.

I've even had a client write salary confidentiality into employment contracts!

Those clauses largely can't be enforced where pay discrimination is in question, but that doesn't stop employers trying.

Here's the way I see it.

For some businesses, it's cheaper to keep replacing people than to fix the pay gaps they've allowed to develop.

And here's the ridiculous cycle.

They don't pay existing employees market rate.

Those employees get approached by recruiters.

They discover they're worth £10k, £20k or even £30k more elsewhere.

They leave.

The employer pays MORE to replace them. 👀

And the whole circus starts again! 🎪

And guess who benefits from this madness?

Recruitment companies like mine!

The irony isn't lost on me.

It's not always deliberate dishonesty. Sometimes it's years of pay freezes, market inflation and inconsistent hiring decisions catching up with businesses.

But let's call it what it is.

A loyalty penalty.

The government's consultation on putting pay in every job advert has just closed. As I told Freelance Informer, I'm all for it. But it's going to make for some very awkward conversations.

And when it lands?

The recruitment snow globe is going to get one almighty SHAKE!

If you're a candidate, this is good news. Know your worth, and don't let loyalty cost you £20k.

If you're in HR, this one's landing on your desk. Pay equality projects are coming, ready or not.

My advice?

Don't wait for legislation.

✅ Benchmark your people NOW
✅ Fix the obvious inequalities
✅ Stop rewarding new starters more generously than the people who've kept your business running

Hiring a country manager feels like commitment.

It is usually premature.

When a new market underperforms, the first instinct is to look at people. Who is in the role, who should be, who can we bring in to fix it.

In my experience, the person is rarely the problem. The organisation dropped them into a market it never diagnosed, with a structure it never built, and expected the hire to make up for both.

Before the first hire, the first partner contract or the first pipeline target, the 4C Channel Framework™ asks four structural questions:
→ Coverage: where will you compete, and through which routes to market?
 → Capability: can your team and partners sell, deliver and support here?
 → Commitment: will you invest at the level the market demands, or only at the level the budget allows?
 → Culture: do you understand how trust is built and decisions are made here?

Most leadership teams answer all four. With opinion, not evidence.

One signed partner is not coverage. An approved budget is not commitment.
Presence comes before narrative. Narrative comes before pipeline. A hire cannot create either.

This week’s edition breaks down why the diagnosis has to come before the hire, not after the first miss.

What would change in your next market entry if you sequenced it that way?

The Friday Footprint

Lenders want your data. Buyers want your data. This week’s five stories all point the same way: the UK SME that can show its numbers wins the funding, the contract and the head start. If a customer or a bank asked for yours on Monday, could you send them by lunchtime?

📦 Packaging emissions now count in tenders
 Packaging carbon builds up across materials, transport and disposal, so swapping one material rarely fixes it. Start by measuring your highest-volume formats. Buyers now score packaging in tenders, and producer responsibility rules reward lighter, more recyclable packs.

🚗 Electric cars hit 31.8% of UK new sales
 October brought 49,155 new battery-electric registrations, up 54% on last year. A Government review could change the 2030 target, so fleet planning needs a total cost of ownership check, not a guess.

💷 Banks have the money, SMEs lack the paperwork
 Global research from Sage and the ICC found that eight in ten SMEs that looked into green finance did not apply. More than 80% of lenders blame unreliable SME data. A clear energy and emissions baseline makes you easier to fund.

🛠️ Green apprenticeships look safer from AI than most
 Only 4.5% of green apprenticeships in England link to roles AI could replace, against 27% overall. Hands-on skills are harder to automate, which matters if you struggle to hire technicians. Treat it as a hiring signal, not a guarantee.

🏟️ The O2 cut emissions 27%, but travel dominates
 The O2 cut emissions 27% per show since 2022. Yet fan travel made up 75.7% of one gig’s footprint, so know what you control and what you only influence. Independent certification helps in tenders.

Proof beats promises. Start with a baseline and everything else gets easier.

Why It Matters: AI Recruiting Software Governance Checklist
Most companies adopt AI recruiting tools the way they adopt any software: a demo, a pilot, a contract. Then six months later, nobody can say who approved the scoring logic, what data the vendor keeps, or what happens when a candidate disputes a rejection.
That’s a governance gap, and in BPO hiring, where AI touches thousands of applicants a month, it becomes a legal and reputational risk quickly.
A checklist worth having before and after go-live:
→ A named owner. One person accountable for the tool’s behavior, not “TA and IT and Legal.”
→ Vendor due diligence. Ask what data trains the model, which inputs drive scores, whether bias audit results exist, and who the sub-processors are.
→ Data rules. Define what candidate data is collected, where it’s stored, how long it’s kept, and how deletion requests are handled.
→ Human override. Document which decisions AI can recommend and which require a recruiter’s sign-off. Rejections shouldn’t be fully automated.
→ Candidate disclosure and appeal. Tell applicants when AI is used and give them a way to request review.
→ Change control. Re-test whenever the vendor updates the model or you change job criteria.
→ Incident process. Know in advance who investigates a bias complaint or a data breach, and how fast.
